sources.summary: All of Hollywood’s biggest stars are in attendance for the Governors’ awards, but nobody gets drunk and the biggest draw is an awkward documentarian Timothée Chalamet was seconds away from getting into trouble. It was just after 6pm in Hollywood and Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was trying to corral a crowd of 700-odd people into sitting down so she could begin the Governors awards ceremony. She jokingly threatened to start calling out anyone still standing by name if they didn’t sit down imminently. Chalamet was the only one left on his feet, circling the table where he was due to sit next to his girlfriend, Kylie Jenner, opposite Tom Holland and Zendaya. Howell Taylor gave him a few seconds’ grace. He looked like the popular kid testing how far he could push a headteacher. The Governors awards had a curiously school-like atmosphere this year. Even the carpet in the Ray Dolby Ballroom was faded and striped. The social structure was much the same: closed-off and insular, with cliques, alliances, legendary enmities and intricate hierarchies of popularity and influence. There were those who seemed entirely comfortable – Chalamet, Holland, Tom Cruise, Matt Damon, Willem Dafoe, Seth Rogen – and others still angling for a better table. Continue reading...

sources.summary: Booth theatre, New York City Liza Colón-Zayas and Thomas Sadoski star in a provocative drama that brings nuance – and dark humor – to the stories of four child sex offenders Fred doesn’t get out much these days, thanks to the incident that put him in a wheelchair. But the elderly man finds joy in small things: the music of Chopin, fruity smoothies prepared by his doting housemate Dee, as well as Nutter Butter cookies. Not everyone sees Fred as harmless. Minutes after we meet him, a man a few decades his junior tells him that he is a fundamentally evil person and describes in cold, chilling detail exactly how he would carry out his murder. Fred is one of four registered sex offenders whose life in a group home is the subject of Downstate, a razor-sharp black comedy by playwright Bruce Norris. As well as Fred (Frances Guinan), the house residents include buff gym rat Gio (Al’Jaleel McGhee), taciturn Felix (Adrian Martinez) and the thespy, Diana Ross-obsessed Dee (K Todd Freeman), a surrogate caretaker for the old man. The men have been somewhat thrown together as an unlikely family, and the yellowing wallpaper and mismatched furniture has certainly seen better days. But the spot is a comfortable enough place for the men to land, although the baseball bat propped up by the front door shows that they are ready for violence if it comes their way. sources.summary: From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants. And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.
